prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Accenture plc" (ticker ACN), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ACN", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Accenture plc
markets: Managed services (application, infrastructure and cloud outsourcing)
Digital marketing and creative services (Accenture Song)

mission.statement: To deliver on the promise of technology and human ingenuity
mission.plain: Accenture wants to help organizations get real results from technology combined with clever people.

about.plain: Accenture is a huge company of experts that big organizations hire to help them use technology. Its people plan new computer systems, build and connect them, and then often keep running them for years. It also runs back-office work like finance and HR for clients, and helps with marketing and cybersecurity. It has more than 814,000 employees working for clients in over 120 countries.
about.customers: Large companies and governments, including most of the world's biggest businesses.
about.everyday: When your bank's app, an airline's booking system or a government benefits website gets rebuilt or moved to the cloud, Accenture is often the firm doing the work behind the scenes.

money.plain: running clients' tech systems and back-office work under multi-year contracts
strategy advice, designing and building new systems, marketing work
building generative and agentic AI into clients' businesses
protecting factories, power grids and industrial systems (Dragos, runZero, NetRise deals in 2026)

result.summary: Accenture has a real but moderate advantage: it is the largest independent IT-services firm, with $74.2B of FY2026 revenue, 317 'Diamond' clients and deep, multi-year relationships that make it the default choice for big, risky transformations. Its scale, partner ecosystem (Microsoft, AWS, Google, SAP, Salesforce, Nvidia) and brand are hard for smaller rivals to match, but the work is people-based and competitive, so margins stay around 15% and AI-driven automation could compress the labor-based model.

pricingPower.evidence: Gross margin has stayed flat at roughly 32% for six years (32.4% FY2021, 32.1% FY2026) and GAAP operating margin in a 13.7%-15.4% band; on the Q4 FY2026 call management said pricing was 'overall stable' for the year but lower in many areas in Q4 and guided FY2027 assuming 'continued intense competition'.

moats.evidence: Accenture is listed in Kantar BrandZ's most valuable global brands and Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies, and its name carries weight with CEOs and boards buying large transformations; it is not a consumer brand.

About half of revenue ($37.3B in FY2026) is managed services under multi-year contracts where Accenture runs clients' systems, and 317 Diamond clients plus 141 quarterly bookings above $100M show sticky relationships; still, contracts are re-competed at renewal.
Its alliances with hyperscalers and software vendors create some ecosystem benefits, but clients do not gain value from other clients using Accenture.

With 814,000+ staff, $1B in R&D and $1B in learning in FY2026, and $4.9B spent on 17 acquisitions, Accenture can field global teams and invest at a scale few rivals match, though Indian firms (TCS, Infosys) have a lower labor cost base.
The IT-services market is large and fragmented with dozens of capable competitors, so there is no natural limit on rivals.
Accenture is the incumbent labor-based model; AI-native and outcome-priced entrants could counter-position against it rather than the reverse.
Decades of delivery playbooks, industry solutions and global delivery networks let it run very large multi-country programs reliably, which is hard for smaller firms to copy.
It has nearly 110,000 AI and data professionals and top-tier partner status with major platforms, but talent and partnerships are available to rivals too.

customers.evidence: Accenture ended FY2026 with 317 Diamond clients (its largest relationships) and a record 141 quarterly client bookings of $100M+, and FY2026 bookings of $84.5B gave a book-to-bill above 1.1, indicating clients keep coming back.

talent.evidence: Great Place to Work ranks Accenture No. 4 on its global World's Best Workplaces list, it is recognized by the Wall Street Journal as a best-managed company, and it trained staff for 46 million hours in FY2026; it recruits at huge scale but pay is below elite strategy firms.

product.evidence: Forbes lists it among the top management consulting firms and it is a top partner for Microsoft, AWS, Google, SAP and Salesforce, but services quality is hard to benchmark and rivals such as Deloitte, IBM and TCS offer similar capabilities.

competitors.name: Deloitte
competitors.note: Technology consulting, systems integration, strategy and cyber; the closest rival in scale and breadth

competitors.name: IBM (IBM Consulting)
competitors.note: IBM Consulting ($21.1B 2025 revenue) competes in systems integration, hybrid cloud and AI services

competitors.name: Tata Consultancy Services
competitors.note: Application development, managed services and outsourcing at lower cost

competitors.name: Capgemini
competitors.note: Consulting, engineering and IT services, especially in Europe

competitors.name: Infosys
competitors.note: Digital transformation, application and infrastructure managed services

competitors.name: Cognizant
competitors.note: IT services and outsourcing, strong in healthcare and financial services

competitors.name: McKinsey & Company
competitors.note: Strategy consulting and growing digital/AI implementation (QuantumBlack)

competitors.name: NTT DATA
competitors.note: IT services and data centers; taken private by parent NTT (9432.T) in 2025

competitors.name: EPAM Systems
competitors.note: Software engineering and digital product development

competitors.name: Genpact
competitors.note: Business process outsourcing and operations services

threats: Generative and agentic AI automating coding, testing and back-office work, shrinking the billable hours that underpin both consulting and managed-services pricing
AI labs, hyperscalers and software firms (e.g. forward-deployed engineering models) selling outcomes directly to clients
Lower-cost Indian rivals (TCS, Infosys, HCLTech, Wipro) competing on price in managed services; management flagged lower pricing in many areas in Q4 FY2026
Weak discretionary consulting demand: consulting revenue grew only 3% in local currency in FY2026
US federal spending cuts weighing on its federal services business
Integration risk from a step-up in acquisitions ($4.9B in FY2026, about $5B planned for FY2027) funded partly by new debt

ceo.name: Julie Sweet
ceo.background: Lawyer (Columbia Law School JD, Claremont McKenna BA); former Cravath, Swaine & Moore partner; joined Accenture in 2010 as general counsel; chair since 2021

c1.evidence: Accenture leads IT services, a large, mature industry growing mid-single digits (Accenture's own FY2026 revenue +5% local currency, FY2027 guide 3%-6%), not an emerging fast-growth one.

c2.evidence: Clients pick it for global scale, breadth from strategy to operations and top-tier alliances (317 Diamond clients), which is hard for small firms to copy but matched in part by Deloitte, IBM and TCS.

c3.evidence: Accenture is the default name in tech consulting among executives and is in Kantar BrandZ's top global brands, but ordinary consumers rarely know what it does.

c4.evidence: Its purpose 'to deliver on the promise of technology and human ingenuity' appears in its materials, but the company is run as a disciplined profit-focused partnership-style business; ten years of execution would matter mainly to clients.

c6.evidence: “consulting, big, corporate” — the impression is mostly neutral to positive among businesspeople (prestige, reliability), with some viewing it as an expensive, long-hours outsourcing firm threatened by AI.

c7.evidence: Enterprise IT services is a very large market being reshaped by cloud and AI, but it grows mid-single digits (Accenture guides 3%-6% for FY2027) and AI may cannibalize labor-based revenue.

c8.evidence: Accenture keeps moving into adjacent areas such as AI, data centers, OT cybersecurity (Dragos, runZero, NetRise in 2026) and marketing (Accenture Song), funded by about $5B a year of acquisitions.

m1.evidence: Julie Sweet has framed Accenture around 'reinvention' and AI, doubling AI and data staff to about 110,000, but her vision is client-led rather than a bold picture of a new industry.

m2.evidence: Sweet is a professional manager (former general counsel) rather than a founder, though she has led the firm since 2019 with long-term investments in AI talent and training.

m4.evidence: Accenture invested $1B in learning and development in FY2026 and is ranked No. 4 on Great Place to Work's global list, yet it has also run large layoffs through business optimization programs.

m5.evidence: The culture is strong at delivery and training, but Accenture invents few products itself; innovation comes mainly through services and acquisitions.

m6.evidence: Sweet is a lawyer by training, not an engineer, and leads as a client-facing executive.

m7.evidence: Sweet is recognized publicly (TIME100 most influential) and the company highlights inclusion and sustainability goals, but stewardship is mainly aimed at clients and shareholders.

m7b.evidence: I could not confirm that Julie Sweet has given a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Sweet is respected and polished but not a distinctive public personality in the mold of Musk or Karp.

m9.evidence: Under Sweet revenue grew from $50,533M in FY2021 to $74,183M in FY2026 with GAAP operating margins steady around 15% and FY2026 free cash flow of $11.6B, though the share price has lagged badly.

m10.evidence: Accenture is cost-disciplined (business optimization programs in FY2023, FY2025, FY2026) but is not known for frugality.

c10.evidence: Its work keeps critical systems of banks, governments and hospitals running for billions of users, but it improves lives indirectly through clients.

p2.evidence: Running large, multi-country technology transformations is hard and important, but many rivals can do similar work.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose every year in the last five: $50,533M (FY2021), $61,594M, $64,112M, $64,896M, $69,673M and $74,183M (FY2026).

f2.evidence: Gross margin was 32.0% in FY2022 and 32.1% in FY2026, and GAAP operating margin 15.2% vs 15.4%, essentially flat with a dip to 13.7% in FY2023.

f3.evidence: At Aug 31, 2026 cash was $12.84B vs total debt $10.11B, FY2026 operating cash flow was $12.36B and shareholders' equity $32.7B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from $9,367M (FY2022) to $11,406M (FY2026) but dipped in FY2023; operating cash flow rose from $9,541M to $12,363M but dipped in FY2024 ($9,131M).

v1.evidence: Accenture is a top choice for very large transformations, but there is no simple, obvious reason to pick it over Deloitte, IBM or TCS for most work.

v2.evidence: Great Place to Work ranks it No. 4 on the global World's Best Workplaces list and it appears on Fortune's World's Most Admired Companies list.

c5.evidence: If it vanished, thousands of large clients would face disruption to systems Accenture runs, but competitors could largely take over the work over time.
